To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) language is an important part of the human experience and is a fundamental aspect of our social and cultural world.

The study of language is a key component of cultural studies and that the linguistic anthropological approach to language in use is a valuable tool for the analysis of literary works and their role in cultural production.

(a) language in use is a locus in which cultural production takes place; (b) the analysis of language in use requires the development of a new interdisciplinary approach that draws on linguistic anthropology and cultural studies; (c) the study of language in use is an important part of literary fieldwork; and (d) this interdisciplinary approach to literary fieldwork can help to illuminate the role of language in use in the production and circulation of literary works.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the way language in use, as a cultural practice, is taken as a subject of literary/cultural production.
the role of language in the production and reproduction of culture.

the ways in which language in use and literary production are mutually constitutive, and with the way in which literary texts can be used to study language in use and the social world in which it is embedded.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
literary/cultural studies can benefit from the attention to language in use and linguistic anthropology can benefit from a greater appreciation of the social life of literary/cultural artifacts.
literary studies, in the broadest sense, can benefit from a more systematic engagement with linguistic anthropology, and vice versa.
this book offers a new way of thinking about the relationship between language and culture and a new way to think about literature and culture.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it seeks to understand the ways in which language in use and the literary text interact with each other in a given cultural context.

we have sought to establish an interdisciplinary approach to literary/cultural studies in the context of linguistic anthropology, and to suggest a number of ways in which such an approach might be carried out.

we have been trying to understand how literary works are produced, consumed, and interpreted, and how they in turn contribute to the production and maintenance of a literary field, a cultural space that is at once a locus of cultural production and an institution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the linguistic and literary fields are not as separate as they might seem.
the study of literature can be enriched by the study of language in use.
literary/cultural studies, in its current state, has not yet taken on board a full appreciation of the role of language in use as an object of study, and that this is a significant omission.
